title: Trump Names Michael Ellis CIA Deputy Director
description_short: An internal, unverified draft isolating the supplied account of Ellis's appointment as CIA deputy director.
description_medium: An internal, unverified draft about the supplied packet's account that Donald Trump named Michael Ellis CIA deputy director on February 3, 2025. The packet describes Ellis as a lawyer and former aide to Representative Devin Nunes and says the role does not require Senate confirmation. CIA's accessible announcement confirms Ellis was sworn in as deputy director and lists earlier national-security posts. The selection date, political characterization and confirmation detail remain unverified here.
description_long:
An internal draft isolates one action from a much broader original entry: the supplied packet says President Donald Trump named Michael Ellis as CIA deputy director on February 3, 2025. The packet describes Ellis as a lawyer and former aide to Representative Devin Nunes and says the deputy role does not require Senate confirmation. CIA's accessible announcement confirms that Ellis was sworn in as deputy director and lists prior service as NSA general counsel, senior director for intelligence programs at the National Security Council, House intelligence committee general counsel and a Navy Reserve intelligence officer.

Those details describe the role and career background; they do not, by themselves, establish when Trump selected him or prove the draft's political-loyalty characterization. The May National Intelligence Council personnel changes, March probationary dismissals and August clearance and Russia-specialist actions in the source packet concern separate events and are excluded from this entry. The source report about the selection timed out during access, so this remains an unverified supplied draft and is not cleared for publication.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Today, Michael Ellis was sworn in as Deputy Director of the Central Intelligence Agency. Deputy Director Ellis previously held a variety of senior national security positions, including General Counsel of the National Security Agency, Senior Director for Intelligence Programs at the National Security Council, and General Counsel of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. He also served as an intelligence officer in the US Navy Reserve.

children.title: Trump Vetoes Yemen War Powers Resolution
children.description_short: Trump vetoed S.J. Res. 7, a resolution concerning U.S. armed forces in hostilities in or affecting Yemen.
children.description_medium: On April 16, 2019, President Donald Trump vetoed S.J. Res. 7, a joint resolution concerning removal of U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in or affecting Yemen. In his message, Trump argued the measure would constrain his commander-in-chief authority and harm U.S. foreign policy. The archive records the veto and his stated rationale; it does not establish the resolution's effects on the conflict or civilian harm.
children.description_long:
On April 16, 2019, President Donald Trump returned S.J. Res. 7 without approval. The joint resolution sought to direct the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in or affecting Yemen, with exceptions. In the veto message, Trump argued that the United States was not engaged in hostilities in Yemen apart from counterterrorism operations against al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and ISIS. He also said the measure would interfere with his commander-in-chief authority and could harm U.S. foreign policy.

This record isolates the Yemen War Powers veto from the separate July arms-export vetoes. It presents the president's explanation as a position in the veto message, not as a neutral finding about the conflict or Congress's authority. The accessible archive establishes the veto message and its contents; it does not measure what followed from the veto, prove its effect on hostilities or establish downstream civilian harm. The message describes the resolution's exceptions only generally, so this draft does not supply additional statutory language.

children.title: Trump Vetoes Three Arms-Transfer Disapproval Resolutions
children.description_short: Trump vetoed S.J. Res. 36, 37 and 38, which would have blocked specified defense export licenses.
children.description_medium: On July 24, 2019, Donald Trump vetoed three joint resolutions that would have blocked specified defense export licenses involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and European partners. His messages argued the restrictions would harm security cooperation and U.S. foreign relations. The official archive identifies each resolution and the proposed transfers; these records do not establish later transfer outcomes, monetary totals or a connection to Jamal Khashoggi.
children.description_long:
On July 24, 2019, President Donald Trump returned three joint resolutions without approval: S.J. Res. 36, 37 and 38. The measures addressed different export licenses and transfers. The archived messages describe components for Saudi Arabia's Paveway production in S.J. Res. 36, Paveway II kits for the United Arab Emirates and European partners in S.J. Res. 37, and the Aurora Fuzing System for the Paveway IV program involving Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom in S.J. Res. 38.

Trump argued that the proposed restrictions would weaken security partnerships, hurt U.S. foreign relations and undermine defense cooperation. In each message he also presented continued licensing as a way to support partners and, in his view, reduce civilian casualties in Yemen. Those are the President's stated reasons, not independent findings about the transfers or their effects. This record corrects the original April date and separates the arms vetoes from the Yemen War Powers veto. The archive does not establish the ultimate disposition of each license, the value of any transfer, a link to Khashoggi's murder or a measurable effect on civilians.

title: Trump Urges Supreme Court to Limit Nationwide Injunctions
description_short: Internal draft of the supplied account that Trump urged the Supreme Court to curb nationwide injunctions.
description_medium: An internal, unverified draft narrows the March 20, 2025 entry to the supplied report that Donald Trump urged the Supreme Court to limit nationwide injunctions. That request is distinct from the frozen entry's sweeping claim that federal judges have no authority over executive action. The source page could not be accessed, so the wording and date remain unverified.
description_long:
An internal draft narrows the frozen entry to a reported March 20, 2025 request by President Donald Trump that the Supreme Court curtail federal judges' ability to issue nationwide injunctions. The supplied packet identifies this as a narrower event than its original claim that Trump declared federal judges lacked all authority over executive action. That broader statement is not supported by the supplied evidence and is not repeated here.

The distinction matters: urging the Court to limit the scope or availability of a remedy is a legal-policy request; it does not mean the Court adopted the request, that a ruling had been issued, or that Trump said courts could never review executive action. The supplied research record links the narrower account to Reuters, but the Reuters page returned HTTP 401 during this session. No literal excerpt was accessed, so the date and account remain supplied claims. This copy is for internal review only; it is not eligible for publication until source text verifies the exact request and wording.
